newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: SERBIA MINISTER DENIES REFORMS WILL MEAN JOB CUTS.
newsitem.headline: SERBIA MINISTER DENIES REFORMS WILL MEAN JOB CUTS.

text.p: Serbia's privatisation minister rejected on Thursday allegations that privatisation would lead to massive lay-offs, saying that surplus labour existed anyway and that reforms would create new jobs.

"Privatisation will not result in redundancies. We already have surplus labour. Any transformed firm means more efficiency and new jobs. But are we ready to do that?" Milan Beko asked representatives of the Serbian power company Elektroprivreda Srbije (EPS) trade union.

EPS said earlier it planned to restructure and privatise and had asked the Belgrade-based Economics Institute and Deloitte & Touche to assess its capital and prepare a plan for its comprehensive restructuring and privatisation by the end of September. It groups 23 companies and employs 61,500 workers.
Beko also cautioned against prejudices towards reforms.

"Those who have money should be allowed to come and invest and we shall have more and cheaper energy. EPS ... needs transformation to make it more efficient," he told EPS trade unions who feared privatisation would bring lay-offs.
Beko said reforms did not only imply reformist legal framework but also a change of mind.
"Now we need to change ideology, to push reforms forward and have no prejudices that foreign partners will come. Let them come and you will be better off."
The minister rejected frequent workers demands for wages only and said those demands put the government under pressure to print money and would lead back to 1993 and hyper-inflation.

"We try to reaffirm an economy in which no free lunch is available. Instead of seeking wages only you must ask the government to ensure that your company will be able to work in future and pay wages and to provide guarantees that restructuring will bring a better life," he said.
The minister insisted that the concept of seeking strategic partners for infrastructure systems was desirable, because that would bring in money and help companies upgrade their technology.
But any strategic partnership deal would be negotiated so that workers remain protected, the minister said.

Early in June, Serbia sealed its first major strategic partnership deal when it sold a 49 percent stake in its Telekom Srbija to Italian and Greek companies Stet and OTE for almost $1 billion. Under the deal, workers were given guarantees there would be no job losses for five years. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 311 4254
